why_wrong.2: Rabindranath Tagore founded Visva-Bharati and was its Acharya, its guiding head. The obvious answer, and the reason the question is asked, but the Vice-Chancellorship went to his son.
why_wrong.3: Indira Devi Chaudhurani was Rabindranath's niece, a writer and musician who preserved his songs.

why_correct: Singaravelu Chettiar organised the first May Day in India, at Madras in 1923, where the red flag was used for the first time in the country. He was among the earliest Indian communists.

why_wrong.1: Chittaranjan Das was the Deshbandhu, a nationalist leader of Bengal and a founder of the Swaraj Party, but not the organiser of May Day.
why_wrong.2: Surendranath Sen is the historian of 1857 who appears elsewhere on this paper, not a labour leader.
why_wrong.3: Gandhi led the national movement and took up workers' causes at Ahmedabad, but May Day is a communist and trade union observance and was not his.

why_correct: Dewan Chamanlal was the first General Secretary of the All India Trade Union Congress when it was founded in 1920.

why_wrong.0: Chittaranjan Das presided over the AITUC in 1923, so he held high office in it, but the first General Secretary was Chamanlal.
why_wrong.2: Lala Lajpat Rai was the first President of the AITUC in 1920. President and General Secretary are different posts, and this is the pair the question is testing.
why_wrong.3: Balgangadhar Tilak was a leader of the extremist wing of the Congress and died in 1920, the year the AITUC was founded.

why_correct: The Madras Labour Union, founded in 1918 by B. P. Wadia, is regarded as the first proper trade union in India, because it had a formal organisation, members and funds.

why_wrong.0: The Workers' and Peasants' Party was a political party of the 1920s, not a trade union.
why_wrong.1: The Centre of Indian Trade Unions was formed in 1970, more than fifty years later.
why_wrong.3: The All India Trade Union Congress was founded in 1920 and is the oldest federation of unions. A federation is a body of unions, so the first single union came first, in 1918.

why_correct: The Eka or unity movement began in 1921 in the districts of Hardoi, Bahraich and Sitapur in Uttar Pradesh, where tenants swore to pay only the recorded rent and not to give forced labour.

why_wrong.1: Madhya Pradesh saw tribal movements of its own but not the Eka movement.
why_wrong.2: Bengal's peasant risings were the Tebhaga movement of 1946 and, earlier, the indigo revolt.
why_wrong.3: Bihar's peasant movement of this period was the Champaran satyagraha of 1917, led by Gandhi against indigo planters.

why_correct: Thirty-three communist and trade union leaders were arrested in the Meerut Conspiracy Case of 1929. The trial dragged on for four years and gave the accused a public platform, which won the movement wide sympathy.

why_wrong.0: 30 is close but short. The figure of 33 is the one recorded for this case.
why_wrong.1: 31 is likewise a near miss.
why_wrong.3: 38 overstates the number. The detail worth carrying away is that the trial began in 1929 and that the government's attempt to break the movement helped publicise it instead.

why_correct: The axis is the imaginary line through the centre of the Earth about which it rotates, and its two ends are the North Pole and the South Pole. It is tilted at 23 and a half degrees from the vertical, which is what gives us the seasons.

why_wrong.0: Both the Equator and the Tropic of Cancer are circles running round the Earth, not points. An axis has to join two points.
why_wrong.2: The Arctic and Antarctic Circles are also lines of latitude, and both lie well away from the poles that the axis actually passes through.
why_wrong.3: The Prime Meridian and the Equator are both great circles on the surface. They cross each other in the Gulf of Guinea, but neither is an end of the axis.

why_correct: The Equator runs east to west round the middle of the Earth, so it separates everything above it from everything below it: the Northern Hemisphere and the Southern Hemisphere.

why_wrong.0: The Eastern and Western Hemispheres are divided by the Prime Meridian and the 180 degree line, which run north to south. Swapping these two is the most common error in this chapter.
why_wrong.2: The Land and Water Hemispheres are a separate idea, centred near France and near New Zealand. They have nothing to do with the Equator.
why_wrong.3: The heat zones are marked out by the Tropics and the Polar Circles, and there are five of them, not two.

why_correct: The Equator is the starting line from which all latitude is measured, so its own latitude is 0 degrees. It is also the longest line of latitude and the only one that is a great circle.

why_wrong.0: 90 degrees is the latitude of the poles, the highest value latitude can reach.
why_wrong.1: 23 and a half degrees is the Tropic of Cancer in the north and the Tropic of Capricorn in the south.
why_wrong.3: 66 and a half degrees marks the Arctic Circle and the Antarctic Circle.

why_correct: The Prime Meridian, 0 degrees longitude, passes through the Royal Observatory at Greenwich in London. It was fixed there by international agreement in 1884 and is the base for Greenwich Mean Time.

why_wrong.0: Paris had its own prime meridian and argued for it at the 1884 conference, but Greenwich was chosen because most shipping already used it.
why_wrong.1: India's own Standard Meridian is 82 and a half degrees east, which passes near Mirzapur, not through New Delhi.
why_wrong.3: Kolkata lies at about 88 degrees east. No meridian of special international standing runs through it.

why_correct: Longitudes are measured east and west of the Prime Meridian, from 0 up to 180 degrees in each direction. They run pole to pole and are also called meridians.

why_wrong.0: North and south of the Equator is how latitude is measured. This is the pair to keep straight: latitude north and south, longitude east and west.
why_wrong.2: All lines of longitude meet at both poles, so the poles cannot be used as a starting point to measure from.
why_wrong.3: Longitudes are counted along the Equator, but they are measured from the Prime Meridian. The question asks about the reference line, not the path.

why_correct: India's Standard Meridian is 82 and a half degrees east, passing near Mirzapur in Uttar Pradesh. It is exactly 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of Greenwich, which gives Indian Standard Time.

why_wrong.0: 75 degrees east passes through western India but is not the standard meridian. Note that a standard meridian is usually chosen as a multiple of 7 and a half degrees, so that the time difference comes out in neat half hours.
why_wrong.1: 90 degrees east lies to the east of India's standard meridian, closer to Bangladesh, and is the standard meridian for that country.
why_wrong.3: 70 degrees east passes near the far western edge of India, well away from the centre a standard meridian should represent.

why_correct: Endogenic forces come from inside the Earth. Endo means within, and these are the forces of earthquakes, volcanoes, folding and faulting that build up the major landforms.

why_wrong.0: Exogenic forces are the opposite: they act from outside, through rivers, wind, glaciers and rain, and they wear landforms down rather than build them.
why_wrong.2: Gravity is a force, and it drives landslides and river flow, but it acts from outside the crust and is grouped with the exogenic forces.
why_wrong.3: Atmospheric forces such as wind and rain act on the surface, which again makes them exogenic.

why_correct: The Himalayas are fold mountains, raised when the Indian plate collided with the Eurasian plate and the sediments of the Tethys Sea were crumpled upward. They are young fold mountains and are still rising.

why_wrong.0: Block mountains are formed by faulting, when a block of land is pushed up or its neighbours drop away. The Vosges and the Black Forest are examples.
why_wrong.1: Residual mountains are old mountains worn down by erosion, such as the Aravallis. The Himalayas are the opposite: young, sharp and still growing.
why_wrong.3: Volcanic mountains are built from erupted lava, like Fujiyama or Kilimanjaro. The Himalayas have no volcanic origin.

why_correct: Erosion is the wearing away of the surface by moving agents such as rivers, wind, glaciers and waves, which loosen material and carry it off. The carrying away is what distinguishes it.

why_wrong.0: Deposition is the laying down of material at the end of the journey. It builds land up rather than wearing it away.
why_wrong.1: Weathering breaks rock down where it stands, without moving it. Weathering plus transport is erosion, so the difference is movement.
why_wrong.3: Sedimentation is a form of deposition, the settling of sediment carried by water or wind.

why_correct: A rift valley forms when the land between two parallel faults sinks, leaving a steep-sided trough. The East African Rift Valley and the Narmada valley in India are examples.

why_wrong.0: Folding bends rock layers upward and downward and builds mountains such as the Himalayas. It does not drop a block of land.
why_wrong.2: Volcanism builds cones and plateaus from erupted material rather than opening a valley by subsidence.
why_wrong.3: Weathering breaks down rock in place and works far too slowly and too shallowly to create a feature on this scale.

why_correct: A plateau is an elevated area with a broad flat top and at least one steep side, so it is commonly called a tableland. The Deccan Plateau is the familiar Indian example.

why_wrong.0: Highland is a loose word for any high ground, including mountains. It is not the specific name for a flat-topped upland.
why_wrong.2: Lowlands are low, level areas such as plains, which is the opposite of a plateau's elevation.
why_wrong.3: A valley is a low area between higher ground, cut by a river or a glacier.

why_correct: Sand dunes are built by wind, which lifts loose sand and drops it where its speed falls. They are typical of deserts such as the Thar, where there is dry loose sand and little vegetation to hold it.

why_wrong.0: Rivers deposit deltas, floodplains and levees. Their sediment is laid down in water, not heaped into wind-shaped ridges.
why_wrong.1: Glaciers deposit moraines and drumlins, made of unsorted rock and clay rather than fine sand.
why_wrong.3: Sea waves build beaches, spits and bars along the coast. Coastal dunes exist, but the wind shapes them even there, not the waves.

why_correct: A delta is formed by river deposition. Where a river meets the sea its speed drops sharply, so the silt it carries settles and builds up land at the mouth. The Sundarbans delta of the Ganga and Brahmaputra is the largest in the world.

why_wrong.1: Wind erosion carves features such as mushroom rocks. Erosion removes material, while a delta is made of material added.
why_wrong.2: Glaciers deposit moraines in cold, high regions. Deltas form at river mouths, usually at sea level.
why_wrong.3: Earthquakes can alter a coastline suddenly, but a delta is built slowly, over centuries, by silt.

why_correct: Moraines are the ridges of rock, gravel and clay that a glacier carries and then dumps as it melts. They are named by where they lie: lateral, medial, terminal and ground moraines.

why_wrong.0: Dunes are heaped by wind in dry regions, not by ice.
why_wrong.2: Deltas are built by rivers at their mouths.
why_wrong.3: Meanders are the loops a river makes across a flat plain. They are a river feature and are formed by erosion and deposition together, not by ice.

why_correct: Weathering is the breakdown of rock in situ, meaning in its own place, by temperature change, water, chemicals or the action of plants and animals. Nothing is carried away, and that is what separates it from erosion.

why_wrong.0: Transportation is the carrying of broken material by water, wind or ice. It is the step that follows weathering, and joining the two gives erosion.
why_wrong.2: Deposition is the dropping of sediment at the end of transport, the last stage rather than the first.
why_wrong.3: Glacier movement is one agent of erosion. Weathering is a process, not the movement of any one agent.

why_correct: After fertilisation the ovary ripens into the fruit, which encloses and protects the seeds. The rule to hold on to is that the ovary becomes the fruit and the ovule becomes the seed.

why_wrong.0: The seed develops from the ovule, not the ovary. The two changes happen together, which is why they are so easily swapped.
why_wrong.2: The ovule is what was there before fertilisation. It is the starting point, not the product.
why_wrong.3: The embryo forms from the fertilised egg inside the ovule, and it sits within the seed. It is one level smaller than what the question asks for.

why_correct: The stamen is the male reproductive part of a flower. It has two parts, the anther, which makes pollen, and the filament that holds it up.

why_wrong.0: The pistil, also called the carpel, is the female part, made of stigma, style and ovary. This is the pair the question is really testing.
why_wrong.2: Sepals are the small green leaf-like parts that protect the bud before it opens. They are not reproductive at all.
why_wrong.3: Petals are the coloured parts that attract insects for pollination. They help reproduction happen but take no part in it themselves.

why_correct: The neuron is the structural and functional unit of the nervous system. Each one has a cell body, dendrites that receive signals and an axon that carries them away.

why_wrong.0: The nephron is the unit of the kidney, not the nervous system. The two names sound alike, which is exactly why they are offered together.
why_wrong.2: Alveoli are the tiny air sacs of the lungs where gases are exchanged.
why_wrong.3: The axon is a part of a neuron, the fibre that carries the impulse away from the cell body. A part of the unit is not the unit itself.

why_correct: Forests and oceans are the main natural carbon sinks. Trees absorb carbon dioxide in photosynthesis and lock it into wood, while the oceans dissolve it and their plankton take it up.

why_wrong.0: Factories are a source of carbon dioxide, releasing it into the air. A sink absorbs; a source emits.
why_wrong.1: Deserts have very little plant life and so absorb very little carbon dioxide.
why_wrong.3: The atmosphere is where the carbon dioxide collects, so it is the reservoir being filled rather than the sink drawing it down.

why_correct: Asthma is a disease of the lungs, in which the airways narrow and become inflamed, making breathing difficult. It is often triggered by dust, pollen or pollution.

why_wrong.0: Heart disease can also cause breathlessness, which is why this seems plausible, but asthma is a disorder of the airways themselves.
why_wrong.1: The liver has no part in breathing. Its diseases include hepatitis and cirrhosis.
why_wrong.3: The kidney is the excretory organ. Its failure affects the filtering of blood, not the passage of air.

why_correct: Ex-situ means off site, conserving a species away from its natural home. A botanical garden does exactly that, as do zoos, seed banks and gene banks.

why_wrong.0: A biosphere reserve protects a whole living landscape where the species already are, so it is in-situ.
why_wrong.2: A national park is also in-situ conservation, protecting habitat in place.
why_wrong.3: A sanctuary likewise protects animals within their own habitat. Three of the four options are in-situ, so the odd one out is the answer.

why_correct: Carbon dioxide is the main greenhouse gas driving global warming. Others such as methane trap more heat per molecule, but carbon dioxide is released in such quantity by burning fuels that its total effect is the largest.

why_wrong.0: Nitrogen makes up most of the atmosphere but is not a greenhouse gas. Being abundant and being warming are quite separate things.
why_wrong.1: Oxygen is essential for life and for burning, but it does not trap heat.
why_wrong.3: Argon is an inert gas making up about one per cent of the air and plays no part in the greenhouse effect.

why_correct: Thalassemia is an inherited disorder in which the globin chains of haemoglobin are not made properly, so the red cells cannot carry oxygen well and the patient becomes anaemic.

why_wrong.0: Insulin is the hormone whose lack causes diabetes. A protein, but the wrong disease.
why_wrong.2: Melanin is the pigment of skin and hair. Its absence causes albinism, another genetic condition, which makes it a tempting distractor.
why_wrong.3: Keratin is the protein of hair, nails and the outer skin.

why_correct: DNA contains adenine, thymine, guanine and cytosine. Uracil replaces thymine in RNA, so it is the base absent from DNA.

why_wrong.0: Adenine is present in DNA and pairs with thymine.
why_wrong.2: Guanine is present in DNA and pairs with cytosine.
why_wrong.3: Cytosine is present in DNA. The one to remember is the swap: thymine in DNA, uracil in RNA.

why_correct: Meiosis is called reductional division because the chromosome number is halved, from diploid to haploid. That halving is what keeps the chromosome number constant from one generation to the next when gametes fuse.

why_wrong.0: Mitosis is equational division: the daughter cells have the same chromosome number as the parent. It is the opposite of what meiosis does.
why_wrong.2: Binary fission is how bacteria and some protists divide, a much simpler process without spindle or chromosomes in this sense.
why_wrong.3: Amitosis is direct division without any spindle or visible chromosomes, seen in some simple cells.

why_correct: In Mendel's monohybrid cross the F2 generation shows three dominant to one recessive, a phenotypic ratio of 3 to 1. That result is what led Mendel to the law of segregation.

why_wrong.0: 1 to 2 to 1 is the genotypic ratio of the same cross, that is one pure dominant, two hybrids and one pure recessive. Genotype and phenotype ratios are the classic mix-up here, because the two hybrids look identical to the pure dominant.
why_wrong.2: 9 to 3 to 3 to 1 is the F2 phenotypic ratio of a dihybrid cross, which follows two characters at once.
why_wrong.3: 1 to 1 is the ratio of a test cross, where a hybrid is crossed with a pure recessive.

why_correct: Auxin causes phototropism. It gathers on the shaded side of a shoot, makes those cells lengthen more, and the unequal growth bends the shoot towards the light.

why_wrong.0: Gibberellin promotes stem elongation and seed germination, but it acts evenly rather than in response to the direction of light.
why_wrong.2: Cytokinin promotes cell division and delays the ageing of leaves.
why_wrong.3: Abscisic acid is the stress hormone. It closes stomata and enforces dormancy, so it slows growth rather than directing it.

why_correct: The medulla oblongata, at the base of the brain stem, controls the involuntary actions that keep us alive: heartbeat, breathing, blood pressure, swallowing, coughing and vomiting.

why_wrong.0: The cerebrum is the seat of thought, memory and voluntary action, which is the opposite of involuntary.
why_wrong.1: The cerebellum controls balance and the coordination of movement. Important and largely unconscious, but not the control of heartbeat and breathing.
why_wrong.3: The hypothalamus regulates body temperature, hunger, thirst and the pituitary gland. Also involuntary, but not these two functions.

why_correct: Cytokinesis is the division of the cytoplasm, which follows the division of the nucleus and completes the making of two separate cells.

why_wrong.0: Karyokinesis is the division of the nucleus, the step that comes first. Karyo means nucleus and cyto means cell, and that is the way to tell the two apart.
why_wrong.1: Mitosis is the whole process of division in body cells, of which cytokinesis is the last stage.
why_wrong.3: Meiosis is the reductional division that makes gametes, again a whole process rather than this one step.

why_correct: In a cactus the leaves are reduced to spines, which cuts the surface area available for transpiration to almost nothing. The stem takes over photosynthesis and stores water, and the spines also deter animals.

why_wrong.0: Broad flat leaves would have a large surface and lose water fast. They suit wet, shady places, which is the opposite of a desert.
why_wrong.2: Air cavities in the stem are an adaptation of water plants such as the lotus, helping them float and get oxygen.
why_wrong.3: Shallow fibrous roots do occur in cacti to catch brief rain, but they gather water rather than conserve it. The question asks about conserving, so the spines are the answer.

why_correct: The molar mass of carbon dioxide is 12 plus 32, that is 44 grams. So 22 grams is half a mole, and since one mole of any gas occupies 22.4 litres at STP, half a mole occupies 11.2 litres.

why_wrong.0: 22.4 litres is the volume of one full mole. That would need 44 grams of carbon dioxide, not 22, so this answer skips the step of finding the number of moles.
why_wrong.2: 2.24 litres is the volume of one tenth of a mole. The decimal point has slipped.
why_wrong.3: 1.12 litres is one twentieth of a mole, again a factor-of-ten slip from the right answer.

why_correct: Water vapour is a greenhouse gas, and in fact the most abundant one. Like carbon dioxide and methane, its molecules absorb the infrared radiation the Earth gives off and re-radiate it back downwards.

why_wrong.0: Oxygen is not a greenhouse gas. Its molecule is made of two identical atoms and cannot absorb infrared in the way a greenhouse gas must.
why_wrong.1: Hydrogen is likewise a two-atom molecule of identical atoms and does not trap heat.
why_wrong.3: Nitrogen makes up most of the atmosphere but is not a greenhouse gas either, for the same reason. The pattern is worth noting: the greenhouse gases here have three or more atoms in the molecule.

why_correct: Bauxite, mainly hydrated aluminium oxide, is the ore of aluminium. It is purified by the Bayer process and then reduced by electrolysis, because aluminium is too reactive to be extracted by carbon.

why_wrong.0: Haematite is an ore of iron, Fe2O3, and the chief one worked in India.
why_wrong.2: Malachite is an ore of copper, a green basic carbonate.
why_wrong.3: Chalcocite is another copper ore, a sulphide. Two of the four options here are copper ores, so it is worth learning ores in groups by metal.

why_correct: Nessler's reagent is the standard test for ammonia. With ammonia or an ammonium salt it gives a brown precipitate, sometimes called Nessler's brown, and the test is sensitive enough to detect very small amounts.

why_wrong.0: Nitrogen dioxide is identified by its own reddish brown colour and its acidic, choking nature, not by Nessler's reagent.
why_wrong.1: Hydrogen sulphide is detected with lead acetate paper, which turns black, and by its smell of rotten eggs.
why_wrong.2: Hydrogen chloride gives dense white fumes with ammonia and turns moist blue litmus red. Note that HCl and NH3 are the classic pair, one acidic and one alkaline, so keep their tests apart.

why_correct: Iron is extracted by thermal reduction in the blast furnace, where carbon and carbon monoxide reduce the oxide ore to the metal. Moderately reactive metals are the ones extracted this way.

why_wrong.0: Silver is a low-reactivity metal found largely in the native state, so it needs no reduction of this kind.
why_wrong.1: Magnesium is highly reactive and is obtained by electrolysis of its molten chloride. Carbon cannot reduce it.
why_wrong.3: Gold is the least reactive of these and occurs free in nature. The rule to apply is that highly reactive metals need electrolysis, moderately reactive ones are reduced by carbon, and the least reactive are found native.

why_correct: Chloroform is CHCl3. Chlorinating it once more replaces its last hydrogen and gives carbon tetrachloride, so this is the one reaction of the four that does not yield chloroform. It consumes it instead.

why_wrong.0: Methane with chlorine in sunlight substitutes one hydrogen at a time, and chloroform appears as the third product in that chain.
why_wrong.1: Methyl chloride is the first product of that chain, and further chlorination carries it on towards chloroform.
why_wrong.2: Dichloromethane is the second product, and one more chlorination gives chloroform directly. Read the question carefully: it asks which does not yield chloroform.

why_correct: A liquid has no fixed shape of its own, so length and area mean nothing for it. Only its volume can expand, which gives one type of thermal expansion, called cubical or volume expansion.

why_wrong.0: Liquids certainly do expand on heating, which is exactly how a thermometer works.
why_wrong.1: 3 is the answer for solids, which have linear, superficial and cubical expansion because a solid holds a definite shape. That contrast is what the question is testing.
why_wrong.3: 2 would fit something with length and area but no volume, which describes nothing. Note that real and apparent expansion are two ways of measuring the same one expansion, not two types of it.

why_correct: In hypermetropia, or long sight, the image forms behind the retina. A convex lens converges the light before it enters the eye and brings the image forward onto the retina.

why_wrong.0: A plano lens has one flat surface, and the term alone does not say whether it converges or diverges. It is not a correction in itself.
why_wrong.2: A concave lens diverges light and corrects myopia, or short sight. This is the pair to keep straight: concave for short sight, convex for long sight.
why_wrong.3: Only one type corrects this defect, so all of these cannot be right.

why_correct: Potassium chloride is an ionic compound, and like dissolves like. Benzene is a non-polar solvent with no ability to pull the ions apart, so KCl is insoluble in it.

why_wrong.1: Glycerol is polar and carries hydroxyl groups, so it can dissolve ionic salts to some extent.
why_wrong.2: Water is the most polar of common solvents and dissolves KCl readily.
why_wrong.3: Alcohol is polar too, and although KCl dissolves in it only slightly, it is not insoluble. Benzene is the only genuinely non-polar option here.

why_correct: Urea is made industrially from carbon dioxide and ammonia at high pressure. The two combine to give ammonium carbamate, which then loses water to form urea.

why_wrong.0: Carbon dioxide and water give carbonic acid, not urea. Nitrogen has to come from somewhere, and neither of these supplies it.
why_wrong.2: NH4 written alone is not a substance. The ammonium ion cannot exist by itself; it needs an accompanying negative ion.
why_wrong.3: Ammonium chloride is a salt used in dry cells and as a flux. It is not the feedstock for urea, which uses ammonia gas directly.

why_correct: Going down group one, the outer electron sits in a larger shell and is better shielded, so it is easier to remove and ionisation energy falls. Order down the group is Li, Na, Rb, Cs, so increasing ionisation energy is Cs, Rb, Na, Li.

why_wrong.1: This puts lithium lowest, but lithium is the smallest of these atoms and holds its electron most tightly, so its ionisation energy is the highest.
why_wrong.2: The order here is jumbled and does not follow the group at all. Sort the elements by position first, then reverse for ionisation energy.
why_wrong.3: This has caesium highest, which is the wrong way round. Caesium's outer electron is furthest from the nucleus and the easiest of all to remove.

why_correct: The becquerel is the SI unit of radioactivity, defined as one disintegration per second. It is named after Henri Becquerel, who discovered radioactivity in 1896.

why_wrong.0: The joule is the unit of energy, not of the rate of decay.
why_wrong.1: Radium is an element, not a unit. The old unit named for a person here is the curie, named after Marie and Pierre Curie.
why_wrong.3: The rutherford is a real but obsolete unit of radioactivity, equal to a million disintegrations per second. It was never the SI unit.

why_correct: A ray striking a surface perpendicularly has an angle of incidence of zero, so it passes straight through without bending. The deviation is therefore zero degrees.

why_wrong.1: 90 degrees would mean the ray turned a right angle, which no glass slab does.
why_wrong.2: 180 degrees would mean the ray came straight back the way it came, which is total reversal, not refraction.
why_wrong.3: 30 degrees suggests some bending, but refraction only occurs when the ray meets the surface at an angle. At perpendicular incidence there is none.

why_correct: Ammonia is dried with quicklime, calcium oxide, because it is a basic drying agent and does not react with the alkaline gas. The rule is that a drying agent must not react with what it dries.

why_wrong.0: Calcium chloride reacts with ammonia to form an addition compound, so it would absorb the gas rather than merely dry it. This is the classic exception to remember, since calcium chloride dries almost everything else.
why_wrong.2: Sulphuric acid is acidic and would react with ammonia at once to give ammonium sulphate.
why_wrong.3: Phosphorus pentoxide is also acidic and would likewise react with ammonia instead of drying it.

why_correct: Thermal conductivity is the rate of heat flow per unit area per unit temperature gradient, so its SI unit is watt per metre per kelvin. It combines power, length and temperature.

why_wrong.0: Watt per metre leaves out the temperature altogether, and thermal conductivity is defined in terms of a temperature difference.
why_wrong.1: The calorie is not an SI unit of energy, and this expression is also missing the temperature term.
why_wrong.2: Multiplying by metre and kelvin instead of dividing turns the unit upside down. Build the unit from the definition and the divisions come out as negative powers.

why_correct: Every even integer can be written as 2n, so every odd integer is one more than an even one, that is 2n plus 1. Whatever integer n you choose, 2n plus 1 is always odd.

why_wrong.0: n alone can be anything, odd or even, so it does not guarantee an odd number.
why_wrong.1: n plus 1 has the same problem. If n is odd then n plus 1 is even, so this can be either.
why_wrong.3: 2n is the general form of an even integer, which is the opposite of what is wanted. Test any form by putting in n equal to 1 and 2 and seeing whether the result is always odd.

why_correct: A quadratic with given sum s and product p of roots is x squared minus sx plus p. That gives x squared minus root 2 x plus one third, and multiplying throughout by 3 clears the fraction to give 3x squared minus 3 root 2 x plus 1.

why_wrong.1: The sign of the middle term is wrong. The formula subtracts the sum of the roots, so a positive sum of root 2 gives a negative middle term.
why_wrong.2: Both the middle sign and the constant sign are wrong here. A positive product of one third must give a positive constant after multiplying by 3.
why_wrong.3: There is a correct option, so none of the above is not needed. Check any answer by dividing through by 3 and reading off the sum and product.

why_correct: Two lines are parallel when the ratios of the coefficients of x and y are equal, so 3 over 2 equals 2k over 5. Cross-multiplying gives 4k equals 15, so k is 15 over 4.

why_wrong.0: 4 over 15 is the answer turned upside down, which comes from cross-multiplying the wrong way. Substitute back to check: with k equal to 15 over 4, the coefficient of y is 15 over 2, and 3 over 2 does equal 15 over 2 divided by 5.
why_wrong.2: 4 over 5 does not satisfy the condition. It looks like the coefficients have been paired up incorrectly.
why_wrong.3: 5 over 4 is close in appearance but wrong. Note that for parallel lines only the x and y ratios must match, while the constant term ratio must differ.

why_correct: The discriminant is b squared minus 4ac, which here is 1 minus 32, that is minus 31. A negative discriminant means the roots are not real, so the equation has no real roots.

why_wrong.0: Roots of opposite signs would need a negative product, that is a negative value of c over a. Here both are positive, and in any case the roots are not real at all.
why_wrong.1: Both positive would need a positive sum of roots, which is minus b over a, but that is minus one half here.
why_wrong.2: Both negative is the closest guess, since the sum is negative and the product positive, but the discriminant settles it first. Always check the discriminant before asking about signs.

why_correct: The nth term is a plus n minus 1 times d. With a equal to 28, d equal to minus 4 and n equal to 7, that is 28 plus 6 times minus 4, which is 28 minus 24, giving 4.

why_wrong.1: 5 would come from using 28 minus 23, which does not match any correct step here.
why_wrong.2: 3 comes from multiplying by 7 rather than by n minus 1. The formula uses one less than the term number, which is the commonest slip in this topic.
why_wrong.3: 7 is simply the value of n copied across rather than the term calculated.

why_correct: In an arithmetic progression each term is the previous one plus the common difference. Starting at 10 and adding 10 each time gives 10, 20, 30, 40.

why_wrong.0: The differences here are 20, 20 and 10, which are not constant, so this is not an arithmetic progression at all.
why_wrong.2: These have a common difference of 5, not 10. The first term is right and the difference is wrong.
why_wrong.3: The differences here are 8, 2 and 10, which are all different. A quick test for any option is to subtract each term from the next and check that you get the same number every time.

why_correct: The diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other at right angles, so they cut it into four right triangles with legs of 8 and 6. The side is the hypotenuse, the square root of 64 plus 36, which is 10 cm.

why_wrong.0: 20 cm is the sum of the halves doubled, or a similar slip. The side must be shorter than the longer diagonal of 16, so 20 is impossible on sight.
why_wrong.1: 8 cm is half the longer diagonal, which is one leg of the right triangle rather than its hypotenuse.
why_wrong.3: 9 cm falls between the two legs, but the hypotenuse is always longer than either leg, so it must exceed 8.

why_correct: The midpoint is the average of the coordinates: x is 2 plus minus 2 over 2, and y is 4 plus minus 4 over 2. Both come to zero, so the midpoint is the origin.

why_wrong.0: This mixes the x of one point with the y of the other rather than averaging.
why_wrong.1: Same error the other way round. The midpoint formula adds the two x values and halves them, then does the same for y.
why_wrong.3: This is simply point B copied out. Notice that A and B are opposite each other through the origin, so the midpoint had to be the origin.

why_correct: By the section formula, the x coordinate of the dividing point is 6m minus 3n over m plus n, and this equals minus 1. That gives 6m minus 3n equal to minus m minus n, so 7m equals 2n and the ratio is 2 to 7. The y coordinate confirms it, since minus 16 plus 70 over 9 is 6.

why_wrong.0: 1 to 3 does not satisfy the section formula. Substituting it gives an x coordinate of 0.75, not minus 1.
why_wrong.1: 3 to 4 gives an x coordinate of about 1.7, which is well away from minus 1.
why_wrong.3: 2 to 5 is the nearest miss and gives an x coordinate of about 0.43. Always substitute your ratio back into both coordinates as a check.

why_correct: From the identity sin squared plus cos squared equals 1, sin X is the square root of 1 minus a squared over b squared. Putting that over a common denominator gives the square root of b squared minus a squared, all over b.

why_wrong.0: The square root has been dropped. Squaring gives b squared minus a squared over b squared, so the root must be taken before dividing by b.
why_wrong.1: b minus a over b comes from subtracting the sides rather than their squares. The identity works on squares, and the square root of a difference is not the difference of the square roots.
why_wrong.3: This makes the same mistake, taking the root of b minus a rather than of b squared minus a squared. A quick check with a 3, 4, 5 triangle settles it.

why_correct: Since tan of an angle times tan of its complement equals 1, the terms pair off: 1 with 89, 2 with 88, and so on, each pair giving 1. That leaves tan 45 in the middle, which is also 1, so the whole product is 1.

why_wrong.0: The product would be zero only if one factor were zero, and tan is zero only at 0 degrees, which is not in this list.
why_wrong.2: 2 would need the pairs to leave something over, but every term pairs off exactly and the leftover tan 45 is itself 1.
why_wrong.3: One half would need some factor less than 1 to remain unpaired. Look for the complementary pairing whenever a product runs from 1 degree up to 89.

why_correct: The height, the distance along the ground and the angle of elevation form a right triangle, so tan 60 equals height over 15. Since tan 60 is root 3, the height is 15 root 3 metres.

why_wrong.1: 10 root 3 would come from a distance of 10 metres. The 15 given in the question is the distance along the ground and must be the one multiplied.
why_wrong.2: 12 root 3 corresponds to a distance of 12 metres, which again is not what was given.
why_wrong.3: 20 root 3 would need a distance of 20 metres. Since the angle is 60 degrees, which is more than 45, the tower must be taller than 15 metres, and that alone rules some options in or out.

why_correct: A tangent meets a radius at 90 degrees, so the quadrilateral formed by the centre, the two points of contact and the outside point has two right angles. Its four angles total 360, so the angle between the tangents is 360 minus 90 minus 90 minus 110, which is 70 degrees.

why_wrong.0: 90 degrees would only occur if the angle between the radii were also 90. The two angles are supplementary, so they are equal only in that one case.
why_wrong.1: 50 degrees does not fit, since 110 plus 50 is 160 rather than 180. The shortcut worth remembering is that the two angles add to 180.
why_wrong.3: 40 degrees is the difference between 110 and 70, not the angle itself.

why_correct: The radius meets the tangent at a right angle, so the centre, the point of contact and the external point form a right triangle with the 5 cm distance as hypotenuse. The radius is the square root of 25 minus 16, that is 3 cm.

why_wrong.1: 5 cm is the distance from the centre to the external point, which is the hypotenuse and so must be the longest of the three.
why_wrong.2: 7 cm is larger than the hypotenuse, which is impossible in a right triangle.
why_wrong.3: 10 cm is larger still. Notice this is the 3, 4, 5 triangle, with the tangent 4 and the distance 5, so the radius is 3.

why_correct: The cube's volume is 22 cubed, that is 10648 cubic centimetres, and seven eighths of it is filled, giving 9317. Each marble has radius 0.25, so its volume is four thirds pi times 0.25 cubed, about 0.0654762. Dividing 9317 by that gives 142296 marbles.

why_wrong.1: 142396 is 100 more than the correct figure and would need a slightly larger filled volume than seven eighths.
why_wrong.2: 142496 is 200 too many. The three wrong options here differ only in the hundreds digit, so the arithmetic has to be carried right through rather than estimated.
why_wrong.3: 142596 is 300 too many. Work with the radius of 0.25 cm, not the diameter of 0.5, since that single slip changes the answer eightfold.
